classification_signals: The paper describes a user study involving 24 adult volunteers navigating a medical complex (page 16).
It compares two different paper maps (original vs. revised) and collects behavioral data using head-mounted cameras (page 16).
Questionnaires were administered to gather self-reported data (page 19).
The 'RESULTS' section (pages 18-30) presents quantitative and qualitative findings from the collected data.
title: Map Design for Complex Architecture: A User Study of Maps & Wayfinding

limitations: The study used a small sample size of 24 participants (page 18).
Participants were paid adult volunteers, not actual patients, potentially reducing anxiety and time pressure compared to real-world scenarios (page 22).
Maps are a single component of an integrated wayfinding system and have limitations in overcoming architectural barriers (page 11, 31).
Map reading is an acquired skill that varies among individuals and may be declining due to increased GPS use (page 12).
The tabloid map size was found to be awkward, and one participant did not unfold it to see detailed information (page 16, 29).
The debate between 'North-Up' and 'Forward-Up' map orientation for hand-held maps is not definitively resolved for all contexts (page 29).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the effectiveness of printed paper maps for wayfinding in a large, complex medical center. While maps were found to assist visitors in reaching their destinations, most participants (22 out of 24) still experienced navigation difficulties. Key findings revealed that architectural barriers, illogical site organization, inadequate signage, and issues with map design (e.g., missing entry points, confusing floor numbering, unclear wing names, awkward map size, and ambiguous symbols) contributed to these difficulties. The study concludes that maps are a beneficial but limited component of wayfinding, and a holistic, integrated wayfinding program is needed to address the inherent spatial complexities of such buildings.
